problemText: Which of the following is a signal word that usually shows a cause/effect pattern in an informational text?
choices: unlike
because
first
solved this by
hints: Signal words point to the pattern. Which word links one event to a result it produces?
Cause/effect shows why one event makes another happen.

problemText: Read this short text: 'Paragraph 1: The school library had a problem — the tables were old and wobbly, and students did not feel safe using them. Paragraph 2: The librarian asked the principal for new tables, and the principal approved the purchase. Paragraph 3: After the new tables arrived, students started spending more time in the library.' What is the organizational pattern of this text?
choices: Chronological, because the events happen one after another in time
Cause/effect, because the wobbly tables caused students to stay away
Problem/solution, because it names a trouble and then explains how it was fixed
Compare/contrast, because it shows the library before and after the purchase
hints: Look for a real trouble that needs to be named first, then a fix that solves it.
The key signal words are 'had a problem' and the approval of new tables.

problemText: A text about how to make a clay pot includes these paragraphs in order: first gathering the clay, then shaping it on a wheel, next letting it dry, and finally firing it in a kiln. Why is chronological order the right pattern for this topic?
choices: Because the topic is solving a problem by listing all the equipment needed to make pottery in the workshop
Because the topic is comparing different ways to make pottery using wheels versus hand-shaping methods
Because the topic is explaining why clay shrinks when it dries out during the kiln-firing stage
Because the topic requires showing the steps in the exact order they must happen
hints: Think about what the topic itself needs. Can you skip steps or do them out of order?
Directions and real processes need events to happen in a particular sequence.

problemText: Read this text: 'Paragraph 1: A hurricane brings heavy rain and high winds to a coast. Paragraph 2: The heavy rain causes flooding in low-lying areas because water has nowhere to go. Paragraph 3: The high winds cause damage to buildings and trees, which then blocks roads and power lines. Paragraph 4: As a result, people lose their homes and power for weeks after the storm.' A student says this text is chronological because it describes events happening during a hurricane. Explain what the student got wrong and name the correct pattern.
choices: The student missed that even though events happen in time, the text is really showing cause/effect because each paragraph explains how one event makes another event happen.

The student confused the topic with the pattern; while hurricanes occur in time, this text is problem/solution because it identifies a weather disaster and then describes ways people prepare to stay safe.
The student overlooked that this is compare/contrast because the text separates the heavy rain damage from the high wind damage and shows how they differ from each other.
The student misread the signal words; the text is actually chronological only for the first half, then switches to cause/effect in the second half, so it uses a mixed pattern overall.
hints: Look at the connecting words: 'causes,' 'because,' 'as a result.' What do these words signal about how the paragraphs connect?
A text can move through time without being chronological. The pattern depends on whether paragraphs just list events or show one event making another happen.

problemText: Two students read a text about how a town planted trees to reduce flooding during heavy storms. Student A says the pattern is problem/solution. Student B says the pattern is before-and-after compare/contrast, since it shows the town before the trees and after the trees. Using what you know about organizational patterns and how they fit their topics, explain which student is correct and why.
choices: Student B is correct, because whenever a text describes conditions at one point in time and then describes conditions at a later point in time, that structure automatically qualifies as a compare/contrast pattern.

Student A is correct, because the text names a real trouble (flooding) and explains the fix (planting trees). Before-and-after is not automatically compare/contrast if a fix is what caused the change.
Both students are correct because the text could be read either way depending on which paragraphs you focus on and how you interpret the author's main purpose.
Neither student is correct, because this text is actually chronological order since it follows the events in sequence through time rather than presenting two separate subjects to examine.
hints: Remember the trap: a before-and-after description is not automatically compare/contrast. Check whether the text names two separate things to weigh against each other.
A pattern fits its topic for a reason. Does this topic call for weighing two separate things, or for explaining how a problem was solved?

problemText: Read this text: 'Paragraph 1: Frogs and toads both have bumpy skin and lay eggs in water, but they are different in many ways. Paragraph 2: Toads have thick, dry bumps and live mostly on land, while frogs have smooth, wet skin and spend most of their lives in water. Paragraph 3: Because toads live on land, they need to come to water only to breed, so they can survive in places where water is scarce. Paragraph 4: Frogs, however, must stay near water or moisture all the time because their skin dries out easily.' Now choose the statement that names the pattern correctly and explains both what makes that pattern fit and what could make a student get confused.
choices: Cause/effect, because the repeated use of connecting words such as 'because' and 'so' in multiple paragraphs signals that the text is showing why one thing happens as a result of another rather than weighing two items.
Chronological order, because the text describes how both animals developed their unique traits over time and explains the sequence of their evolution from a common ancestor.

Compare/contrast, because it sets frogs and toads side by side to show how they are alike and different, even though some paragraphs use 'because' and 'so' which might make a student think the text is cause/effect.
Problem/solution, because the text identifies the challenge that each animal faces in finding appropriate habitats and presents the physical adaptations as the solution to that challenge.
hints: The whole text's job is to set two separate creatures side by side and show how they differ. That is compare/contrast. But look at those connecting words—why might they fool a reader into seeing a different pattern?
A text can use signal words from more than one pattern. The key is to ask: what is the main job of the whole text? Is it to weigh two things, or to show why one thing causes another?

problemText: What is the difference between an author's purpose and an author's topic? Give your answer in one sentence.
choices: An author's purpose and topic are the same thing because both refer to the main idea that the author wants to communicate to readers.
An author's topic is always more important than the author's purpose because readers care more about what a text is about than why it was written.
An author's purpose is the reason the text was written, while the topic is what the text is about.
An author's purpose is about facts and information, while the topic is about the author's personal opinions and beliefs.
hints: Think about what the lesson said: 'Author's purpose is the reason a text was written, not its subject.'
The lesson showed that two texts about the same event can have different reasons for being written.

problemText: Read this sentence from a sports newsletter: 'The track team finished third in the district championships last Saturday.' Does this sentence use neutral or persuasive language, and why?
choices: Persuasive language, because it uses the word 'finished' instead of a different verb that would sound more neutral or objective.
Persuasive language, because it tells readers that they should care about the track team's performance and should support them.
Neutral language, because it is a short sentence.
Neutral language, because it reports what happened without judging the outcome or asking the reader to do anything.
hints: Look for judgment words or calls to action. Does this sentence tell you how to feel, or just what happened?
The lesson says neutral words 'report information without pushing the reader anywhere.'

problemText: Read this announcement: 'The school library will add ten new computers in the study area starting next month.' Which sentence below would change the purpose of this announcement from informing to persuading?
choices: Every student who wants to improve their grades should take advantage of these new computers as soon as they arrive.
The library will purchase the computers from a company that sells educational equipment and has a strong reputation in schools.
The computers will be available during all hours that the library is open to students and staff.
The library is conveniently located on the second floor of the main building next to the media center.
hints: Persuasive language tells readers what they should do or what they should believe. Which choice contains a command or a judgment?
Look for words that urge the reader to act or words that tell the reader what is worthwhile.

problemText:
Read the two passages below about a new community garden. Both describe the same project, but which one is written to persuade, and what specific proof shows this?

Passage 1: 'The community garden opened on Maple Street this spring. Volunteers spent four weekends preparing the soil and building raised beds. Forty families signed up to grow vegetables in the garden, and fifteen families are currently on a waiting list to join.'

Passage 2: 'The community garden finally opened on Maple Street, and it is going to change our neighborhood. Volunteers generously gave their time to prepare the soil and build raised beds for this worthy project. Forty families are already growing vegetables, and even more are waiting to get in. You should sign up today and become part of this thriving community effort.'
choices: Passage 1 is written to persuade, proven by the fact that it describes a community garden and mentions that volunteers helped build it.
Passage 2 is written to persuade, proven by the command 'You should sign up today and become part of this thriving community effort.'
Passage 1 is written to persuade, proven by the word 'currently' and the mention of a waiting list showing that many people want to join.
Passage 2 is written to persuade, proven by mentioning that families signed up to grow vegetables and that the garden is located on Maple Street.
hints: Remember: naming a purpose is only half the job. You must also point at the exact word or detail that proves it.
Look for sentences that tell the reader what to do or that use judgment words like 'worthy' or 'finally.'

problemText:
Read this passage about a school's new homework policy:

'The school raised the homework limit to ninety minutes per night this semester. Students in math classes report that the extra practice helps them understand challenging concepts better. However, students in science classes say the increased workload makes them feel stressed, and some say they have less time to play sports. The policy has benefits and drawbacks that affect different students in different ways.'

What does the author's choice of selected details—which benefits and drawbacks to include—tell you about the author's purpose?
choices: The author is trying to persuade readers to support the new homework policy by showing only the positive effects it has on math students.
The author is trying to persuade readers that homework should be banned because it makes most students feel stressed and prevents them from playing sports.
The author is trying to inform readers by reporting outcomes on both sides of the issue, not just favoring one side.
The author is trying to inform readers that the policy is bad by listing more drawbacks than benefits in the passage.
hints: The lesson says: 'A passage that reports outcomes on more than one side is informing about those outcomes; a passage that lines up only the details that favor one side is persuading.'
Notice what the author chose to include: benefits from math and drawbacks from science. Does this pick only one side, or both?

problemText:
Read these two excerpts about the same city park renovation project:

Excerpt A: 'The city will invest $2 million in the park renovation. The project will include new walking paths, updated playground equipment, and improved lighting. The renovation is expected to take fourteen months and is scheduled to begin in September.'

Excerpt B: 'The city is investing $2 million to transform our neglected park into a safe gathering place. New walking paths and updated playground equipment will finally give families a reason to visit. The improved lighting will protect everyone who uses the park after dark. This project deserves community support, and residents should volunteer for the work and attend the planning meetings starting in July.'

Which excerpt is written to persuade, and what combination of word choice and selected details (or calls to action) proves this?
choices: Excerpt A is written to persuade, because it mentions that the project will cost $2 million and will take fourteen months to complete.
Excerpt B is written to persuade, because it mentions walking paths and playground equipment that will be built in the park.
Excerpt A is written to persuade, because it lists specific details about what will be renovated and provides a timeline for the work.

Excerpt B is written to persuade, because it uses judgment words like 'neglected' and 'safe,' includes a call to action ('residents should volunteer'), and selects only benefits while leaving out any drawbacks.
hints: Look for more than one signal of persuasion: judgment words, calls to action, and one-sided selected details all point in the same direction.
The lesson teaches that purpose must be proven by multiple clues—word choice AND selected details AND what the passage leaves out. Which excerpt shows all three?

problemText: Two accounts describe the same field trip to a museum. Before you can compare what each account includes and leaves out, what must you check first?
choices: You must confirm that both accounts describe the same event—the same day, the same place, the same trip.
You must count how many sentences each account has to see which one is longer.
You must decide which account sounds more like a personal letter and which sounds more like an official report.
You must identify which account includes numbers and which one includes feelings.
hints: The lesson teaches a step-by-step method for comparing accounts. What comes first?
Look back at the worked examples—what do they do before making any lists of what each account adds?

problemText:
Read both accounts of the same soccer game.

Source A (a player's text to a friend): "Our team won 3–2 against Lincoln Middle School on Wednesday afternoon, and I scored two of our goals. I was so nervous before the game that I almost threw up in the locker room."

Source B (the school's sports newsletter): "The girls' soccer team defeated Lincoln Middle School 3–2 on Wednesday afternoon in a competitive match that came down to the final minutes."

Which fact appears in BOTH accounts?
choices: The player's nervousness before the game in the locker room.
The team won 3–2 against Lincoln Middle School on Wednesday afternoon.
The match came down to the final minutes.
The player scored two of the team's three goals.
hints: Shared facts appear in both sources using the same or very similar language. Look for the sentence that repeats across both accounts.
A detail that only one account mentions—like feelings or nervousness—is not a shared fact.

problemText:
Read both accounts of the same science project fair.

Source A (a student's journal entry): "Today was our school's science fair, and I set up my water filtration project on table seven. I spent three hours there answering questions about my experiment, and my little sister came to watch and brought me a juice box when I was thirsty."

Source B (the science teacher's report): "Our school held its annual science fair today. Forty-two students displayed projects covering topics from robotics to plant biology. The fair ran from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. in the gymnasium."

What detail appears in Source A but NOT in Source B?
choices: The fair ran from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m.
The projects covered robotics and plant biology topics.
The student's sister brought juice during the fair.
The science fair took place at the school today.
hints: Look at what Source A includes that Source B does not mention at all.
A personal account like a journal entry often includes details about feelings and people close to the writer. An official report often leaves those details out.

problemText:
Read both accounts of a community garden volunteer day.

Source A (a volunteer's blog post): "Twenty-five neighbors worked together on Saturday morning to plant spring vegetables in our community garden beds. Everyone was smiling and chatting as we dug in the soil, and by lunchtime we had already planted tomatoes, peppers, squash, and lettuce. It felt like we were doing something that really mattered to our neighborhood."

Source B (the parks department's monthly report): "On Saturday morning, twenty-five volunteers planted spring vegetables in the community garden on Maple Street. The team completed planting in all six raised beds and worked for three hours, starting at 9 a.m. The parks department provided all tools and seed stock."

Both accounts describe the same volunteer day. Which statement BEST explains how they differ in what they include?
choices: Source A emphasizes the emotional experience and sense of community purpose, while Source B emphasizes the location, the number of beds planted, the duration of work, and the source of equipment.
Source A names the specific vegetables that were planted but Source B does not mention them at all, suggesting Source B was written by someone who did not attend the event.

Source A reports only positive observations about the volunteers' mood and accomplishment, while Source B includes only factual measurements of time and resources that make the day sound less meaningful.
Source A focuses on how the volunteers felt and what they accomplished together, while Source B focuses on details like the number of beds, the time worked, and who provided the supplies.
hints: Both accounts report the same event. Neither contradicts the other. The difference is in selection and emphasis—what each writer chose to spend words describing.
What does Source A emphasize through repeated words and sentences? What does Source B emphasize through numbers and logistics?

problemText:
Two accounts describe the same book club meeting.

Source A (a member's email to a friend): "The Riverside Book Club met on Tuesday evening to discuss our latest read. Everyone had finished the book except Marcus, and the group spent two hours talking about how much they loved the main character's journey. We laughed so hard at one scene that someone spilled coffee on the carpet."

Source B (the club's official meeting notes): "Tuesday evening book club meeting. Attendance: 8 members. Book discussed: The Wanderer's Path. Meeting ran 7 p.m. to 9 p.m. The club voted to read The Mountain House next month."

Which of the following correctly identifies a shared fact and explains why it is shared?
choices: The group spent two hours talking is shared because Source B shows the meeting was 7 p.m. to 9 p.m.
The Riverside Book Club met on Tuesday evening to discuss their latest read is shared because both accounts use these same words.
Everyone had finished the book except Marcus is shared because both accounts mention Marcus.
Someone spilled coffee is shared because both accounts describe events that happened during the meeting.
hints: A shared fact must be a detail that both accounts state or clearly confirm. Look for what both sources agree on, even if they use different words to say it.
Source B gives the meeting time as 7 p.m. to 9 p.m., which is two hours. Does Source A's claim about two hours match that information?

problemText:
Read these two accounts of a school assembly.

Source A (student council president's speech, printed in the school newspaper): "Last Friday's assembly brought our entire school together for our annual awards ceremony. I felt proud watching sixth graders, seventh graders, and eighth graders stand on stage to receive certificates for art, music, sports, and academic achievement. The auditorium was packed, and you could hear the crowd cheering every time someone's name was called."

Source B (a substitute teacher's note in the classroom log): "Attended mandatory assembly on Friday. Approximately 500 students and staff present. Program lasted 45 minutes. Awards were presented in four categories. Two students had technical difficulties with their microphones during the program."

Based on both accounts, which statement is true?
choices: The accounts disagree about whether awards were given in multiple categories, so they cannot be describing the same assembly because Source A names specific categories while Source B does not.

Both accounts describe the same assembly with the same awards ceremony, but Source A emphasizes the feeling of pride and unity while Source B emphasizes the size of the crowd and the length and technical details of the program.

Source B reports a technical problem during the assembly, while Source A reports only positive feelings about the awards, which means Source A deliberately left out negative information to make the assembly sound better than it was.

Source A is more accurate because it focuses on students' emotional experiences and accomplishments, whereas Source B only records factual data like attendance numbers and duration without capturing the meaningful purpose of the event.
hints: Remember: different details and different emphasis are not the same as disagreement. Check whether both accounts state the core event the same way.
Notice what each writer chose to include: one focuses on emotion and pride, the other on numbers and logistics. What does the lesson call this difference?

problemText: According to the lesson, what two things must be attached to a specific claim in order for it to count as supported?
choices: A fact and the writer's opinion
A reason and confident wording
Evidence and a main claim
A reason and evidence
hints: Think about what the lesson calls the two building blocks that back up a claim.
Evidence is the specific fact or example, and a reason explains why the claim should be believed.

problemText: Read this short argument: 'Our school should start a lunch exchange program. Students who bring lunch from home could trade items they do not want with other students. This would reduce food waste because students are more likely to eat food they actually chose instead of throwing it away.' Which specific claim in this argument is supported by a reason and evidence?
choices: This would reduce food waste because students are more likely to eat food they actually chose instead of throwing it away
Our school should start a lunch exchange program because it would be simple to organize and manage during lunch periods
Students who bring lunch from home could trade items they do not want with other students since many students pack extra snacks
A lunch exchange program would improve student happiness because students get to interact with their classmates during the lunch period
hints: Look for a sentence that has both a reason (why) and evidence (a fact or explanation) right next to it.
The word 'because' in the sentence signals that a reason is being given.

problemText: Read this passage: 'The school should require all students to bring reusable water bottles instead of buying plastic ones. Plastic bottles take hundreds of years to break down in the environment. Students who use the same bottle every day create far less trash than students who buy a new bottle each week. Reusable bottles are also obviously the coolest thing anyone could carry.' A student claims that the specific claim about plastic bottles breaking down slowly is supported, while the specific claim about reusable bottles being 'the coolest thing' is not. Explain which one is correct and why, based on the definition of a supported claim.
choices: The student is wrong about both claims; neither one has evidence attached to it
The student is correct; both claims are actually supported, so the student made an error
The student is correct; the plastic breakdown claim has a reason and fact, but the 'coolest' claim does not
The student is wrong about the first claim; confident words like 'obviously' always mean a claim is supported
hints: Check whether each claim has a real reason and fact next to it, or whether it just stands alone.
Remember that confident words like 'obviously' or 'coolest' are tone, not evidence.

problemText: A student is tracing this argument: 'The school cafeteria should add a salad bar with fresh vegetables. Fresh vegetables are healthier for students than the fried foods the cafeteria serves most days. Students who eat more vegetables have better energy and focus in their afternoon classes, and research shows that diets high in vegetables lower the risk of heart disease later in life. Adding a salad bar would definitely be popular with everyone.' The student identifies three specific claims and must sort each as supported or not supported. What is the correct sort for all three?
choices: All three claims are supported because they all sound important
The first and third claims are supported; the second claim is not supported
Only the second claim is supported because it mentions research
The first and second claims are supported; the third claim is not supported
hints: Go through each claim one by one and check whether reason and evidence actually appear in the text right around it.
The last claim has words like 'definitely' and 'popular,' but do those same words come with a real fact or reason?

problemText: Read this argument: 'The school should invest in solar panels on the roof of the main building. Solar panels would lower the school's electricity costs because they convert sunlight into power and reduce how much energy the school has to buy from the power company. Installing solar panels is also a way to teach students about renewable energy. Solar energy is the future of electricity generation, and solar panels would definitely inspire every single student in the building to care about science.' A student must trace this argument and sort each claim. The student notices that one claim uses confident language like 'definitely' and 'every single student,' and wonders if that confident wording means the claim is supported. Using the lesson's definition, explain whether confident wording makes a claim supported or not supported, and identify which claim in this passage demonstrates that principle.
choices: Confident wording is not evidence; the solar-panels-inspire-students claim is not supported because no reason or fact backs it up
Confident wording makes a claim supported because words like 'definitely' are a form of evidence; the solar-panels-inspire-students claim is supported
Confident wording makes a claim supported only if the claim is also about money, like the electricity-cost claim
Confident wording makes a claim not supported; the electricity-cost claim is therefore not supported even though it has real evidence
hints: The lesson warns against mistaking confident words like 'obviously' or 'definitely' for actual reasons and evidence.
Look at what comes right before and after the claim about inspiring students—is there a real reason and fact, or only strong-sounding words?
